review.summary: This paper investigates how training-point allocation strategies—specifically uniform area-proportional pixel sampling, boundary-excluding interior sampling, privileged patch-first ('oracle') sampling, and two-stage model-guided proposal/uncertainty sampling—interact with frozen annual satellite embeddings (Google AlphaEarth Foundations v2.1) versus seasonal Sentinel-2 optical composites when recovering small palustrine wetland patches (0.2–1 ha) across four US National Wetlands Inventory (NWI) projects. Using a fixed budget of 2,000 labeled pixel positions and Random Forest / logistic regression classifiers evaluated at a 5% upland false-positive rate (FPR), the planned single-split comparison finds that patch-first allocation improves small-patch recovery (>=50% pixel coverage) by 12.8 percentage points (pp) for embeddings versus 1.2 pp for optical features (an interaction of 11.6 pp), even as aggregate pixel-level IoU remains virtually unchanged (~48.6%). However, extensive follow-up sensitivities reveal that the initial split was an outlier: across a four-split rotation, both predictors benefit from patch-first sampling (+8.4 pp for embeddings, +3.9 pp for optical; interaction +4.5 pp), optical predictors actually touch more small patches under an any-overlap (>=1 pixel) criterion while embeddings cover more patches at >=50% extent, most of the oracle gain can be replicated without new patches via inverse-patch-size sample weighting or per-core sample quota matching, and operating thresholds fail to transfer reliably across geographic projects.

score_reasons.correctness: The statistical analyses, exhaustive sensitivity checks, and self-critical interpretations are highly rigorous and transparently show how the primary single-split interaction (+11.6 pp) attenuates under 4-split rotation (+4.5 pp) and validation threshold replay, though the primary pre-registered design suffered from cross-core sample quota confounding, sub-MMU training polygons, and using an optical teacher to select points for the embedding classifier.
score_reasons.verifiability: Data processing, AlphaEarth v2.1 decoding, Sentinel-2 harmonization, classifier hyperparameters, and bootstrap procedures are specified in thorough detail, though exact core center coordinates are deferred to external repository files and Figure 2 is visually clipped on the right edge.
score_reasons.novelty: While object-vs-pixel training allocation (Corcoran et al., 2015), size-weighted losses for small waterbodies (Zhou et al., 2025), and AlphaEarth evaluations on wetlands and small ponds (Ryan et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026) exist, isolating the pixel-allocation interaction between frozen embeddings and seasonal optical predictors on held-out small patches is a solid incremental contribution.
score_reasons.generality: The study spans four distinct US wetland regions, multiple sample budgets, and two decoders, but generality is constrained by strong split-to-split variance, reversal of predictor rankings between any-overlap and >=50% patch coverage, and poor cross-region threshold transferability.
score_reasons.usefulness: The findings offer actionable guidance for practitioners using geospatial embeddings: pixel-level IoU hides large shifts in small-patch recovery, inverse-size weighting recovers most of the patch-first sampling benefit on fixed pixels, and decision thresholds require local calibration.
score_reasons.clarity: Tables and technical definitions are precise, but the text and abstract are heavily overloaded with exploratory protocol amendments (v1–v11), internal audit-log minutiae (e.g., commit-timing codes), and repetitive boilerplate caveats that obscure the main scientific narrative.

research_question.question: How does training-point allocation (uniform pixel sampling versus patch-first and model-guided sampling) interact with annual satellite embeddings versus seasonal optical predictors in recovering small mapped wetland patches (0.2–1 ha) at a fixed upland false-positive rate?
research_question.predictable_reason: That equal-patch sampling or inverse-area weighting improves small-object recall relative to uniform pixel sampling follows from sampling probabilities, and that smoother annual embeddings favour >=50% patch coverage while noisier optical pixels favour any-overlap detection aligns with known spatial coherence properties, though the split sensitivity and cross-region threshold transfer failures were not predictable a priori.

main_issues.issue: Design confounding in the primary 'oracle' vs. 'area' comparison: uniform area sampling pools pixels across all training cores, whereas patch-first sampling draws more heavily from cores containing many small polygons and originally included sub-MMU (<0.2 ha) polygons. The paper's own exploratory controls show that matching per-core positive counts accounts for +4.4 pp of the +12.8 pp embedding gain and restricting training polygons to >=0.2 ha reduces recovery by 2.4 pp.

Over-reliance on a single small split (16 test cores, 227 patches) for the primary planned claim: in the 4-split rotation (Section 4.5), all three new rotations yielded interactions (+4.7, -0.4, +1.2 pp) below the lower bound of the primary conditional 95% interval [4.9, 18.5], demonstrating that fixed-training-set block bootstrap intervals substantially understate split selection uncertainty.

Mismatched teacher representation in the planned practical allocation arms: the planned 'Image proposals' and 'Uncertainty' policies used a 100-tree optical Random Forest to select second-stage training points even when fitting the annual embedding classifier, making the negative result for planned proposals on embeddings (-0.2 pp) an artifact of cross-representation mismatch rather than a fair test of self-guided active sampling.

Severe narrative clutter from protocol versioning and audit-log minutiae: sections 3.1, 3.5, and 7 include internal workflow references (e.g., 'v1–v11', 'E03/E62 commit-timing corrections and E64's late-loaded presentation helper', 'gpt-6-astra') and repetitive negative disclaimers in almost every paragraph, which should be streamlined into standard scientific prose.

Figure defects and missing visual assets: in Figure 2 (figures/threshold-transfer.svg), the right panel ('Validation threshold replay') is clipped at the right edge, cutting off data points above ~7.4% FPR, the panel title, and the x-axis label parenthesis; both attached SVG figures have excessive blank whitespace at the bottom; and Appendix G links to an unattached file (figures/coverage-by-size.svg).

strengths: Exceptional scientific honesty and self-critique: the paper proactively executes and foregrounds split rotations, validation threshold replays, core-quota controls, and coverage sensitivities that substantially temper its own headline single-split finding.

Clear demonstration of an important practical phenomenon: aggregate area-weighted segmentation metrics (pixel producer's accuracy and IoU) remain virtually identical (~48.6%) while small-patch (0.2–1 ha) recovery shifts by 8–13 percentage points.

Insightful geometric distinction between predictors: seasonal optical classifiers touch more small wetland patches (>=1 pixel overlap), whereas annual embeddings recover more patches at >=50% and >=75% area coverage.

Well-designed mechanistic controls showing that inverse-patch-size sample weighting on standard area-sampled pixels recovers most of the oracle patch-first advantage without requiring new training patches.

closest_prior_work.citation: Liu, D., Zhu, X., Holgerson, M., & Xu, X. (2026). Utility and Explainability of Earth Embeddings in Mapping Small Ponds. IEEE Geoscience and Remote Sensing Letters, DOI: 10.1109/LGRS.2026.3740204.
closest_prior_work.difference: Evaluates AlphaEarth Foundations and TESSERA embeddings on small ponds (0.1–1 ha) and shows AEF omits small waterbodies due to spatial smoothing unless fused with Sentinel-1/2, whereas the reviewed paper isolates pixel-level training sample allocation (area vs. patch-first vs. uncertainty) at fixed upland FPR.

closest_prior_work.citation: Ryan, S., Powell, M., Ling, J., & Wen, L. (2026). Streamlining Wetland Vegetation Mapping with AlphaEarth Embeddings: Comparable Accuracy to Traditional Methods with Cleaner Maps and Minimal Preprocessing. Remote Sensing, 18(2), 293.
closest_prior_work.difference: Compares AlphaEarth embeddings with multi-source optical/SAR predictors for wetland vegetation communities using cluster-screened samples, but does not evaluate training-point allocation policies or held-out small-patch recovery rates.

closest_prior_work.citation: Corcoran, J., Knight, J., Pelletier, K., Rampi, L., & Wang, Y. (2015). The Effects of Point or Polygon Based Training Data on RandomForest Classification Accuracy of Wetlands. Remote Sensing, 7(4), 4002–4025.
closest_prior_work.difference: Compares single-pixel, fixed-window, and polygon-object training for wetland Random Forest mapping by changing both feature aggregation and output mapping units, whereas this paper holds pixel predictors and the 10 m output grid fixed to isolate sample allocation.

closest_prior_work.citation: Zhou, P., Foody, G., Zhang, Y., Wang, Y., Wang, X., Li, S., Shen, L., Du, Y., & Li, X. (2025). Using an Area-Weighted Loss Function to Address Class Imbalance in Deep Learning-Based Mapping of Small Water Bodies in a Low-Latitude Region. Remote Sensing, 17(11), 1868.
closest_prior_work.difference: Introduces inverse-area loss weighting for deep learning segmentation of small waterbodies on PlanetScope imagery, whereas the reviewed paper compares patch-first sampling and inverse-size weighting across frozen satellite embeddings versus seasonal Sentinel-2 features.

closest_prior_work.citation: Sharma, A., Kharbanda, A., Anand, A., Mishra, R., Zhang, Y., & Biswas, S. (2026). Wetland Mapping Under Boundary Uncertainty with AlphaEarth Embeddings, LiDAR and Sentinel. Preprints.org, 202610.0964.
closest_prior_work.difference: Examines 20 m boundary-zone exclusion when mapping wetlands with AlphaEarth embeddings, LiDAR, and Sentinel-2, but focuses on pixel-level F1/overall accuracy rather than patch-first training allocation and small-patch recovery.
